title: How to Choose Who Goes First Without Putting Anyone on the Spot
author: Nick Martin
summary: Nick Martin argues that asking a room 'who wants to start?' hands the decision to whoever is most comfortable speaking, so the same confident person goes first every time and quietly sets the starting point for the whole discussion. He offers six facilitation moves that decide for the room, kindly: let a harmless rule choose, have everyone write first and then read, use pairs before the room, warn a named person before you ask, go first yourself with a deliberately rough answer, and let the room's layout set the order. His warning move refines the 'pose, pause, pounce, bounce' technique by naming the person before the pause so they can prepare while everyone else knows they are not first. A worked 90-minute session shows how each move matches how exposing the question is. The takeaway is that choosing who speaks first is a design decision, not something to leave to volunteering.
points: Martin's core claim is that the first answer steers everything after it, so leaving the opener to volunteers lets one confident voice frame the problem session after session.
Harmless rules (next birthday, furthest traveled) and room layout let a neutral device pick the speaker so nobody feels singled out.
Writing a sentence first and then reading it aloud, or sharing a pair's idea instead of one's own, lowers the exposure of speaking and keeps the first answer from steering the rest.
Naming one person 30 seconds ahead is the respectful form of cold-calling, and it lets everyone else relax because they know they are not first.
Match the move to how exposing the question is, and go first yourself with a rough one-sentence answer when you most need honesty from the room.
quotes: Whoever speaks first sets how long people talk, how honest they get, and often which part of the problem everyone ends up discussing.
Asking “who wants to start?” leaves the decision to the room, and the room leaves it to whoever is most comfortable talking.
Reading your own words is far easier than thinking out loud on the spot. The hard part is already done on paper.
People share a pair’s idea more easily than their own. If it lands badly, it belonged to both of them.
Cold-calling puts someone on the spot in front of everyone. A name with 30 seconds’ notice gives them time to think, and most of the time they’re glad to be asked.
Going first sets the length and the level of honesty for everyone after you. It’s a common go-to, and it sets the tone quickly.
Mine’s not polished, but...” does two jobs. It shows the room how long to go on for. And it gives everyone permission to be imperfect, which is usually what was stopping them.
Over 90 minutes you never asked who wants to start, and nobody sat through a 10-second silence. The confident person still spoke plenty. The first answer to each question came from someone different.
